title: Human Brain
think_prompt: How can one organ receive sensory information, support thinking and memory, control movement, balance the body, and regulate vital involuntary actions?
definition: The brain is a major part of the central nervous system and contains several regions specialised for different coordinating functions.
description: This subunit studies the brain as a whole and then focuses on its three main parts: the cerebrum, cerebellum and medulla oblongata.
image_description: 16:9 Grade 11 biology overview illustration of the human brain in side view inside a simplified head silhouette. Clearly distinguish the cerebrum, cerebellum and medulla oblongata using subtle contrasting regions, but keep labels minimal because each part is taught separately later. Show the spinal cord continuing downward from the medulla to establish orientation. Clean scientifically accurate textbook style suitable for a classroom smart board.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to identify the three large brain regions they can distinguish visually before revealing their names.
quick_check: Name the three main parts of the brain studied in this subunit.

title: Brain as a Whole — Position and Protection
think_prompt: Why does such an important and delicate coordinating organ need more than one form of protection?
definition: The brain lies within the cranium and is surrounded by three protective linings called meninges.
description: The brain is protected by the cranium and surrounded by three meninges. It forms the upper major part of the central nervous system and continues inferiorly toward the spinal cord through the medulla oblongata.
key_points: Cranium|Three meninges|Protection|Central nervous system|Continuity with spinal cord
image_description: 16:9 anatomical educational cutaway of a human head showing the brain inside the cranium. Clearly show the skull around the brain and three thin protective meninges surrounding the brain as layered coverings. Indicate the brain's position in the cranial cavity and its continuation toward the spinal cord, but avoid microscopic membrane details. Clean Grade 11 science style with readable callouts.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to identify the hard outer protection and the protective linings around the brain.
quick_check: State two structures that protect the brain.
answer: The cranium and the three meninges.
remarks: Protection scene; detailed spinal-cord protection remains for SU06

title: Overall Structure of the Brain
think_prompt: Looking at the external and longitudinal views of the brain, how can it be divided into major regions?
definition: The brain is composed of three main parts: the cerebrum, cerebellum and medulla oblongata.
description: The cerebrum forms the largest upper region, the cerebellum lies below the posterior part of the cerebrum, and the medulla oblongata forms the lower brain-stem region continuous with the spinal cord. The peripheral region of the brain is grey matter and the interior contains white matter.
key_points: Cerebrum|Cerebellum|Medulla oblongata|Peripheral grey matter|Interior white matter
image_description: 16:9 precise labelled side-view and simplified longitudinal-view brain diagram. Clearly label Cerebrum, Cerebellum and Medulla oblongata and show the spinal cord continuing from the medulla. Add one simple inset or visual cue showing grey matter peripherally and white matter internally, without introducing microscopic detail. Large clear labels, Grade 11 textbook style.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to label the three main brain parts and describe their relative positions.
quick_check: What are the three main parts of the brain?

title: Cerebrum — Structure and Function
think_prompt: Why is the cerebral cortex highly convoluted, and what major activities depend on the cerebrum?
definition: The cerebrum is the largest and most highly developed part of the brain.
description: The cerebrum is divided into left and right hemispheres. Its cortex is highly convoluted, increasing surface area. The left cerebral hemisphere controls the right half of the body and the right hemisphere controls the left half. The cerebrum perceives and identifies sensory information, stores information, supports higher mental activities such as learning, intelligence and thinking, and controls voluntary muscle contraction.
key_points: Largest brain part|Two hemispheres|Convoluted cortex|Sensory perception and identification|Memory/storage|Learning intelligence thinking|Voluntary muscle control|Opposite-side control
image_description: 16:9 scientifically accurate cerebrum-focused educational diagram. Show a large lateral brain view with the cerebrum highlighted, plus a simple top or frontal inset showing left and right cerebral hemispheres. Emphasize the highly folded cortex. Add clean icons or small callouts for sensory perception, learning/thinking, memory and voluntary muscle control. Include a subtle crossed-control cue showing left hemisphere → right body and right hemisphere → left body. Avoid advanced cortical lobe mapping.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to connect visible structural features of the cerebrum with its listed functions.
quick_check: State two important functions of the cerebrum.
answer: It perceives and processes sensory information and controls voluntary muscle contraction; it also supports higher mental activities such as learning, intelligence and thinking.
remarks: Technical cerebrum scene based on textbook scope

title: Cerebellum — Structure and Function
think_prompt: What must the nervous system do to keep the body balanced while voluntary muscles are moving?
definition: The cerebellum is a brain region involved in body balance and the coordination of voluntary muscle activity and movement.
description: The cerebellum lies just below the posterior part of the cerebrum. It consists of two hemispheres, with grey matter in the outer layer and white matter internally. Its functions include maintaining body balance, controlling voluntary muscle activity and helping maintain body movement.
key_points: Below posterior cerebrum|Two hemispheres|Outer grey matter|Inner white matter|Body balance|Voluntary muscle activity|Body movement
image_description: 16:9 cerebellum-focused Grade 11 biology visual. Show a lateral brain view with the cerebellum clearly highlighted below the posterior cerebrum. Include a small simplified section indicating outer grey matter and inner white matter, plus visual cues of a person balancing and coordinated voluntary movement. Keep the cerebrum and medulla visible only for orientation, not as the focus.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to relate the cerebellum's position and structure to its major movement-related functions.
quick_check: State two functions of the cerebellum.
answer: It maintains body balance and helps control voluntary muscle activity and body movement.

title: Medulla Oblongata — Structure and Function
think_prompt: Which brain region must continue working even when you are not consciously thinking about heartbeat, breathing, coughing or swallowing?
definition: The medulla oblongata is an important brain centre controlling several vital involuntary and reflex activities.
description: The medulla oblongata is located in the lower brain, anterior and internal to the cerebellum, and continues toward the spinal cord. It controls involuntary activities such as heart-beat rate and respiration rate and controls reflex actions such as vomiting, coughing and swallowing.
key_points: Lower brain region|Continues to spinal cord|Heart-beat rate|Respiration rate|Vomiting|Coughing|Swallowing|Involuntary control
image_description: 16:9 scientifically accurate brain-stem illustration with the medulla oblongata highlighted between the upper brain regions and spinal cord. Use small clean functional callouts for heartbeat, breathing, coughing, swallowing and vomiting. Keep the visual physiological but age-appropriate, and do not turn it into a reflex-arc diagram. Grade 11 textbook-quality presentation.
interaction_instruction: Give several functions and ask students which ones are controlled by the medulla oblongata.
quick_check: Name two activities controlled by the medulla oblongata.
answer: Examples include heart-beat rate, respiration rate, vomiting, coughing and swallowing.
remarks: Do not expand into reflex-arc mechanism here

title: Compare the Three Main Brain Parts
think_prompt: How can you distinguish the cerebrum, cerebellum and medulla oblongata using both position and function?
definition: The three main brain parts can be compared by their location, structural features and major functions.
description: Use a comparison table to distinguish the cerebrum, cerebellum and medulla oblongata. Focus on relative location, major structural features and the main functions required at this level.
key_points: Feature|Cerebrum|Cerebellum|Medulla oblongata;Location|Largest upper brain region|Below posterior cerebrum|Lower brain, near cerebellum and spinal cord;Structure|Two hemispheres, highly convoluted cortex|Two hemispheres, outer grey and inner white matter|Brain-stem region continuous with spinal cord;Main functions|Sensory processing, higher mental activities, voluntary muscle control|Balance and coordinated voluntary movement|Heartbeat and respiration rates, vomiting, coughing, swallowing
image_description: 16:9 comparison-table visual with three equal columns headed Cerebrum, Cerebellum and Medulla Oblongata. Place a small accurate highlighted brain sketch at the top of each column. Use rows for Location, Structural features and Main functions. Keep the table concise with large smart-board-friendly typography and no advanced neuroanatomy.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to read across each row and state one difference between each pair of brain regions.
quick_check: Which brain part mainly maintains body balance?

title: Identify the Brain Part
think_prompt: If you know what function is affected, can you identify the most relevant brain part?
definition: A brain part can often be identified from its characteristic location or major function.
description: Classify familiar functions using the three main regions: higher mental activity and voluntary muscle control → cerebrum; body balance and coordinated voluntary movement → cerebellum; heart-beat rate, respiration rate and reflex actions such as coughing or swallowing → medulla oblongata.
key_points: Learning/thinking → Cerebrum|Voluntary muscle control → Cerebrum|Balance → Cerebellum|Coordinated movement → Cerebellum|Heartbeat/respiration → Medulla oblongata|Coughing/swallowing → Medulla oblongata
image_description: 16:9 retrieval-practice visual showing six unlabeled function cards or icons: thinking/learning, voluntary arm movement, body balance, coordinated walking, heartbeat/breathing and coughing/swallowing. Beneath them show three empty destination zones labelled Cerebrum, Cerebellum and Medulla Oblongata. Do not place the answers in the image; students should classify each function.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to assign each function to cerebrum, cerebellum or medulla oblongata and justify one answer.
quick_check: Which brain part is most directly associated with higher mental activities such as learning, intelligence and thinking?
